title: Chapter 25. Of Counsel
paragraphs: How fallacious it is to judge the nature of things by the ordinary and inconstant use of words appears in nothing more than in the confusion between counsel and command, which arises from the imperative manner of speech used in both — and on many other occasions besides. The words 'do this' belong to the man who is commanding, but also to the man giving counsel, and to the man exhorting; and yet there are few who do not see that these are very different things, or who cannot tell them apart when they observe who is speaking, to whom the speech is directed, and on what occasion. But when men find such phrases in others' writings, and are unable or unwilling to consider the circumstances, they sometimes mistake the precepts of counsellors for the precepts of those who command, and sometimes the reverse — whichever best fits the conclusions they want to infer, or the actions they approve. To avoid such mistakes, and to give the terms 'commanding,' 'counselling,' and 'exhorting' their proper and distinct meanings, I define them as follows.

COMMAND is where a man says, 'Do this,' or 'Do this not,' expecting no other reason for it than the will of him who says it. From this it follows plainly that the one who commands aims at his own benefit; for the reason of his command is his own will alone, and the proper object of every man's will is some good to himself.

COUNSEL is where a man says, 'Do this,' or 'Do not this,' and draws his reasons from the benefit that arises to the one he is addressing. From this it is plain that the one who gives counsel aims (whatever else he may intend) at the good of the one to whom he gives it.

Therefore one great difference between counsel and command is that command is directed to the benefit of him who issues it, and counsel to the benefit of another. From this arises another difference: a man may be obliged to do what he is commanded, as when he has covenanted to obey; but he cannot be obliged to do as he is counselled, because the harm of not following it is his own. And if he should covenant to follow it, then the counsel is turned into the nature of a command. A third difference between them is that no man can claim a right to be of another man's counsel, since he is not to claim any benefit by it for himself; but to demand the right to counsel another implies a wish to know his designs, or to gain some other good for oneself — which (as I said before) is the proper object of every man's will.

It is also incident to the nature of counsel that the man who asks for it cannot in equity accuse or punish it. To ask counsel of another is to permit him to give such counsel as he thinks best; and so a man who gives counsel to his sovereign (whether a monarch or an assembly) when asked for it cannot in equity be punished for it, whether or not it agrees with the opinion of the majority, provided it bears on the proposition under debate. For if the mind of the assembly could be known before the debate has ended, they ought neither to ask nor to take any further counsel; the mind of the assembly is the resolution of the debate, and the end of all deliberation. And in general, he who asks for counsel is the author of it, and so cannot punish it; and what the sovereign cannot, no one else can. But if one subject gives counsel to another to do anything contrary to the laws, whether that counsel comes from evil intention or merely from ignorance, it is punishable by the commonwealth — because ignorance of the law is no good excuse where every man is bound to take notice of the laws to which he is subject.

EXHORTATION and DEHORTATION are counsel accompanied with signs in the giver of a vehement desire that it be followed — or, to put it more briefly, counsel vehemently pressed. The man who exhorts does not draw out the consequences of what he advises and tie himself in this to the rigour of true reasoning; he urges the man he is counselling on to action — just as the man who dehorts deters him from it. So in their speeches they pay attention to the common passions and opinions of men in drawing out their reasons, and make use of similitudes, metaphors, examples, and other tools of oratory to persuade their hearers of the utility, honour, or justice of following their advice.

From this it may be inferred, first, that exhortation and dehortation are directed to the good of the man who gives the counsel, not of the one who asks for it — which is contrary to the duty of a counsellor, who (by the definition of counsel) ought to look not to his own benefit but to the benefit of the man he advises. That he directs his counsel to his own benefit is plain enough from the long and vehement urging, or from the artful manner of giving it: such effort, not having been required of him, and so proceeding from his own motives, is directed principally to his own benefit, and only incidentally — or not at all — to the good of the one being counselled.

Second, that the use of exhortation and dehortation lies only in addressing a multitude. When the speech is addressed to one man, he may interrupt and examine the reasons more strictly than can be done in a multitude — which is too numerous to enter into dispute and dialogue with the one who speaks indifferently to them all at once. Third, that those who exhort and dehort where they were asked to give counsel are corrupt counsellors, and as it were bribed by their own interest. For however good the counsel they give may be, the one who gives it is no more a good counsellor than the one who hands down a just verdict for a reward is a just judge. But where a man may lawfully command, as a father in his family or a leader in an army, his exhortations and dehortations are not only lawful but also necessary and laudable. But then they are no longer counsels, but commands; which, when they are for the carrying out of harsh labour, sometimes necessity, and always humanity, requires to be sweetened in delivery by encouragement, and given in the tone and phrase of counsel rather than in the harsher language of command.

Examples of the difference between command and counsel we may take from the forms of speech that express them in Holy Scripture. 'Have no other gods but me; make to thyself no graven image; take not God's name in vain; sanctify the Sabbath; honour thy parents; kill not; steal not,' and so on, are commands; because the reason for obeying them is drawn from the will of God our King, whom we are obliged to obey. But the words 'sell all thou hast, give it to the poor, and follow me' are counsel; because the reason for doing so is drawn from our own benefit — namely, that we shall have 'treasure in heaven.' The words 'Go into the village over against you, and you shall find an ass tied, and her colt; loose her, and bring her to me' are a command, because the reason for the act is drawn from the will of their Master. But the words 'Repent, and be baptised in the name of Jesus' are counsel; because the reason for so doing tends not to any benefit of God Almighty (who shall still be king in whatever way we rebel), but to our own — we have no other means of avoiding the punishment hanging over us for our sins.

Just as the difference between counsel and command has now been derived from the nature of counsel — which consists in drawing out the benefit, or harm, that may come to the one being counselled, by the necessary or probable consequences of the action proposed — so the differences between apt and inept counsellors may also be derived from the same source. For experience being only the memory of the consequences of like actions formerly observed, and counsel being only the speech by which that experience is made known to another, the virtues and defects of counsel are the same as the virtues and defects of the intellect. To the person of a commonwealth, his counsellors serve in the place of memory and mental discourse. But with this resemblance between the commonwealth and a natural man, there is one important dissimilarity: a natural man receives his experience from the natural objects of sense, which act on him without any passion or interest of their own; whereas those who give counsel to the representative person of a commonwealth may have, and often do have, their own particular ends and passions — which makes their counsels always suspect, and many times unfaithful. So we may set down as the first condition of a good counsellor that his ends and interests be not inconsistent with the ends and interests of the one he counsels.

Second: because the office of a counsellor, when an action comes into deliberation, is to make plain the consequences of it, in such a way that the one being counselled may be truly and clearly informed, he should put forward his advice in such a form of speech as makes the truth appear most plainly — that is, with as firm a reasoning, in as proper and clear language, and as briefly, as the evidence will permit. So rash and unevident inferences (such as are drawn only from examples, or from the authority of books, and which are not arguments of what is good or evil, but witnesses of fact or of opinion); obscure, confused, and ambiguous expressions; and also all metaphorical speech tending to stir up the passions — because such reasoning and such expressions are useful only to deceive, or to lead the one being counselled toward ends other than his own — are repugnant to the office of a counsellor.

Third: because the ability to counsel proceeds from experience and long study, and no man is presumed to have experience in all the things necessary to be known for the administration of a great commonwealth, no man is presumed to be a good counsellor except in matters he has not only had much practice in but has also much meditated and reflected on. For since the business of a commonwealth is to preserve the people at home and defend them against foreign invasion, we shall find that it requires great knowledge of the disposition of mankind, of the rights of government, and of the nature of equity, law, justice, and honour — not to be attained without study. And it requires knowledge of the strengths, commodities, and locations both of their own country and of their neighbours, as also of the inclinations and designs of all nations that may in any way harass them; this is not attained without much experience. Of these matters, not only the whole sum but every one of the particulars requires the age and observation of a man of years, and of more than ordinary study. The wit required for counsel, as I have said before, is judgement; and the differences between men on this point come from different education — some to one kind of study or business, others to another. When for the doing of any thing there are infallible rules (as in engines and buildings, the rules of geometry), all the experience in the world cannot equal the counsel of the man who has learnt, or found out, the rule. And where there is no such rule, the man with most experience in that particular kind of business has the best judgement in it, and is the best counsellor.

Fourth: to be able to give counsel to a commonwealth in a matter that touches another commonwealth, it is necessary to be acquainted with the intelligence and the letters that come from there, and with all the records of treaties and other transactions of state between them — which none can be but those whom the representative shall think fit. From this we may see that those who are not called to counsel cannot have any good counsel to offer in such cases.

Fifth: supposing the number of counsellors to be equal, a man is better counselled by hearing them apart than in an assembly; and that for many reasons. First, hearing them apart, you get the advice of every man; but in an assembly, many of them deliver their advice with an 'aye' or 'no,' or with their hands or feet, not moved by their own sense but by another's eloquence, or for fear of displeasing some who have spoken (or the whole assembly) by contradiction, or for fear of appearing duller than those who applauded the opposite opinion. Second, in an assembly of many there cannot but be some whose interests are contrary to the public's, and these interests make them passionate, and passion makes them eloquent, and that eloquence draws others into the same advice. The passions of men, which apart are moderate, like the heat of a single brand, in an assembly are like many brands that inflame one another — especially when they fan one another with orations — and they end by setting the commonwealth on fire under the pretence of counselling it. Third, in hearing every man apart, one may examine (when need arises) the truth or probability of his reasons and of the grounds of his advice, by frequent interruptions and objections; which cannot be done in an assembly, where (on every difficult question) a man is rather astonished and dazzled by the variety of speech on it than informed of the course he ought to take. Besides, there can hardly be an assembly of many called together for advice in which there are not some who have the ambition to be thought eloquent, and also learned in politics, and who give their advice not with care for the matter at hand but for the applause of their motley orations, made of the various coloured threads, or shreds, of authors. This is at best an impertinence, taking up the time of serious consultation; and in the private way of counselling apart, it is easily avoided. Fourth, in deliberations that should be kept secret (and there are many occasions in public business for this), the counsels of many — especially in assemblies — are dangerous; and so great assemblies are forced to commit such affairs to smaller numbers, and to those persons most versed in the matter and in whose fidelity they have most confidence.

To conclude: who is there who so far approves the taking of counsel from a great assembly of counsellors that he would wish for, or accept, their pains when the question is the marriage of his children, the disposing of his lands, the governing of his household, or the managing of his private estate — especially if there are among them some who do not wish his prosperity? The man who does his business with the help of many prudent counsellors, each consulted apart in his proper element, does it best — as the man who at tennis uses able partners, placed in their proper stations. The man who uses his own judgement only does it next best — as the man who has no partner at all. But the man who is carried up and down to his business in a framed council, which cannot move except by the plurality of consenting opinions, the execution of which is commonly (out of envy or interest) hindered by the dissenting party, does it worst of all — like one who is carried to the ball, though by good players, in a wheelbarrow or other frame, heavy in itself and slowed besides by the conflicting judgements and efforts of those who push it; and all the more so, the more they are who put their hands to it; and most of all when there is one or more among them who wish him to lose. And though it is true that many eyes see more than one, this is not to be understood of many counsellors, but only when the final resolution is in one man. Otherwise, because many eyes see the same thing in different lines, and are apt to look askance toward their private benefit, those who do not want to miss their mark, though they look about with two eyes, never aim except with one. And so no great popular commonwealth has ever been kept up except by some foreign enemy who united them, or by the reputation of some one eminent man among them, or by the secret counsel of a few, or by the mutual fear of equal factions — and not by the open consultations of the assembly. And as for very small commonwealths, popular or monarchical, no human wisdom can uphold them longer than their potent neighbours' jealousy lasts.
